Picture a square or rectangular open courtyard — like a peaceful garden — inside a monastery or convent. Now imagine a covered walkway running along all four sides of that courtyard. This walkway has a solid wall on one side (the outer wall of the building) and a row of arched openings or columns on the other side, so you can see into the garden as you walk. It has a roof overhead, protecting you from rain or harsh sun.

That covered walkway — wrapping all the way around the open courtyard like a frame — is called a cloister.

The shape is always the same: a closed loop. Walk in any direction and you'll eventually come back to where you started. The courtyard it surrounds is usually a simple garden — sometimes with a fountain, a well, or just grass. The arches facing the garden are often beautifully carved. The overall effect is one of calm, quiet, and enclosure.

You'll find cloisters in medieval monasteries, convents, abbeys, cathedrals, and even some old universities across Europe and beyond.

Monks or nuns used the cloister as a daily living space. Because it had a roof, they could walk, pray, read, and meditate there regardless of weather. It also served as a passageway connecting the different parts of the monastery — the church, the dining hall, the sleeping quarters, and so on. The cloister was the heart of monastic life: a quiet, protected space for the mind to turn inward.

Over time, the word "cloister" grew to mean not just the walkway itself but the entire monastery or convent — the whole enclosed religious community. So when someone is said to have "entered the cloister," it means they gave up ordinary life and joined a monastery or convent as a monk or nun.

Example: "She left everything behind and entered the cloister at the age of twenty."

Outside of religion and architecture, "cloister" is also used figuratively to describe any secluded, sheltered place that is cut off from the noise and business of the outside world. It suggests quiet, retreat, and separation.

Example: "He spent his years in the cloister of academia, far removed from the struggles of ordinary life."

Here, "cloister" is used loosely to describe the university as a kind of bubble — a protected world of its own.

This adjective flows naturally from the noun and is very commonly used. Something or someone that is cloistered is sheltered, secluded, and shut away from the wider world.

  • A cloistered life — a life of quiet retreat, away from worldly affairs.
  • Cloistered nuns — nuns who live in strict enclosure and have very little or no contact with the outside world.
  • A cloistered upbringing — being raised in a way so sheltered that you have little experience of how the real world works.

The word always carries a sense of deliberate withdrawal — of walls (literal or figurative) that keep the outside world at bay.

A cloister is a covered, arched walkway enclosing a courtyard, found in monasteries and similar buildings — and by extension, it means the entire monastery itself, or any secluded place sheltered from the world.
